title: Learning Lesson 3: Concentration is hard
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This lesson covers the second of Chew's four universal learning bottlenecks: concentration is hard, and it fatigues over the course of a day for every human being, not just distractible students. Stuart opens with a relatable diagnostic question — do you feel less sharp in sixth period than third period? — to establish that this fatigue is real and near-universal rather than a personal deficiency. He explains the fix as overlearning and practicing knowledge to the point of automaticity, illustrated through the example of experienced drivers who can hold conversations or take calls while driving without crashing, because the skill itself has become automatic and no longer taxes limited concentration. He brings in Dan Willingham's observation that the brain will avoid effortful thinking whenever possible, reframing overlearning not as extra credit but as the mechanism that frees up concentration for genuinely new thinking. The lesson closes with concrete overlearning tactics students can apply across their classes: self-quizzing, giving pretend lectures, using new vocabulary outside class, and quizzing classmates.
points: Stuart normalizes concentration fatigue by asking students whether they feel measurably less sharp late in the school day, reframing it as a universal cognitive limit rather than a personal failing.

The driving analogy — an experienced driver who can converse or take a call without crashing — makes the abstract concept of automaticity concrete: overlearned skills stop taxing limited concentration.

He cites Dan Willingham's principle that the brain will avoid effortful thinking whenever possible, reframing overlearning as the mechanism that frees up scarce concentration for new problems rather than a shortcut.
The lesson ends with four concrete, repeatable overlearning tactics students can use in any class: self-quizzing, pretend lectures, using new vocabulary outside class, and quizzing classmates.
quotes: Who in this room feels like they are at least 1% less intelligent during sixth hour than they are during, say, third hour? That's not because your long-term memory has become damaged throughout the day — it's because your ability to concentrate has become fatigued.
As the day goes on, if we've been working hard to concentrate all day long, our attention becomes fatigued. That's true for all human beings — none of us can concentrate endlessly.
Because after years of driving, you overlearn the knowledge and skill that goes into it — and this makes the process pretty fantastically automatic.
There's a cognitive scientist in Virginia named Dan Willingham who puts it this way: Whenever we can, we will AVOID thinking. Why!? Because the concentration required by thinking is hard!
When you overlearn material, you don't have to concentrate as hard to think about it — and this makes learning a lot less of a drag.
